case_info.scenario: A 51-year-old male with a complaint of a 4-week history of redness and swelling of the right temporal bulbar conjunctiva was referred for evaluation of a choroidal lesion in the right eye. He had a history ofBRAFV600 E mutation-positive, superficial spreading-type cutaneous melanoma (CM) on the chest with metastasis to a sentinel lymph node 3 years ago. He was treated at the time of diagnosis with excision of the primary tumor with clear margins and axillary lymph node dissection. He also had a papillary thyroid carcinoma 1 year earlier treated with thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine-131. He had a follow-up visit with his oncologist 2 days before his presentation to our ocular oncology clinic and he did not have any systemic findings suggestive of recurrence of his previous malignancies. The best-corrected visual acuity after a new refraction was 20/30 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Anterior segment examination of the right eye revealed temporal conjunctival hyperemia with dilated episcleral vessels. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed a partially pigmented choroidal lesion, measuring 26 × 21 × 8.1 mm, superotemporally extending to the macula associated with exudative retinal detachment inferiorly (Figure 1A). Ultrasonography showed an acoustically solid lesion with prominent intralesional vascularity with irregular internal structure on B-scan and mid to low internal reflectivity on A-scan (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Fundus photography showing a partially pigmented choroidal lesion located superotemporally (yellow arrowhead), extending to the macula with associated exudative retinal detachment inferiorly (white arrowhead). B, B-scan ultrasound image of the lesion showing an acoustically solid lesion with prominent intralesional vascularity with an irregular internal structure (asterisk), measuring 26 × 21 × 8.1 mm, with subretinal fluid that overlies the lesion and extends inferiorly (arrowhead) on B-scan.
case_info.explanation: Solitary choroidal metastasis secondary to primary cutaneous melanoma of the chest Solitary choroidal metastasis from CM is rare with only a few case reports in the literature.1-4It can be challenging to differentiate solitary choroidal metastases of CM from primary choroidal melanoma through clinical examination and imaging studies. Due to recent advances in immunotherapy and targeted therapies, it is important to differentiate the 2 tumors as treatment options might differ accordingly. Though cutaneous and choroidal melanomas have similar embryonic origin and histological features, their epidemiological and cytogenetic characteristics differ.5 Genetic testing can assist in distinguishing CM from primary uveal melanoma since they have genetically distinct initiating mutations with different genetic mutational profiles. CMs most commonly have activating mutations in BRAF kinase. In contrast, uveal melanomas typically lack BRAF mutations and are characterized by mutations in GNAQ, GNA11, BAP1, EIF1AX, and SF3B1.5In our case, the cytopathology came out to be consistent with melanoma with tumor cells positive for SOX10 and Melan A and negative for TTF1 and PAX8 as assessed by immunohistochemical staining. An allele-specific polymerase chain reaction assay revealed the tumor was positive forBRAFc.1799T>A V600E mutation, which was the key to the diagnosis of metastatic CM. Three days after the choroidal fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) procedure, the patient noticed a new dark-colored skin nodule on his right neck. FNAB of this lesion also proved to be melanoma. He also had a whole-body workup and had no further systemic metastases. He was diagnosed with choroidal and cutaneous metastasis from CM of the chest. Two agents of immunotherapy, nivolumab and ipilimumab, were started. At examination after 3 months of immunotherapy, the metastatic choroidal lesion had regressed to a flat scar, measuring 26 × 21 × flat mm, and the exudative retinal detachment was resolved. After 10 cycles of treatment, he discontinued immunotherapy due to adverse effects. His metastatic cutaneous lesion on the right neck completely resolved, too. Choroidal metastasis from CM is reported to be treated with radiation, enucleation, chemotherapy, and most recently with immunotherapy and targeted therapies.1-5Rieth et al3reported a case with systemic metastasis from CM who received immunotherapy after external beam radiotherapy with BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Choroidal metastasis regressed within 1 month. CMs are shown to be responsive to immunotherapy, especially combined nivolumab and ipilimumab therapy, with a 58% response rate and 52% at 5-year survival rate.6To the best of our knowledge, our case is the first report that shows the effectiveness of immunotherapy-alone treatment in the eye, showing an eye-preserving option for choroidal metastasis from CM. In this case, based on the previous history of multiple systemic cancers without any known systemic metastasis and clinical and imaging findings of choroidal lesion, FNAB (option C) will be the first step to confirm the diagnosis and plan management. After the correct diagnosis, the management options of plaque radiotherapy (option A), enucleation (option B), or observation while receiving systemic therapy if it is metastasis (option D) could be considered. After the metastasis was diagnosed, immunotherapy was started as a globe-preserving treatment due to the detection of another metastatic site in the neck and to avoid the possible ocular adverse effects of plaque radiotherapy. The patient was followed up closely, and external beam radiotherapy or enucleation was reserved as a second line if immunotherapy fails. Plaque brachytherapy was deferred as the lesion exceeded the size limits.7This case shows an eye-preserving outcome for choroidal metastasis from CM associated with immunotherapy alone in the eye. At last examination 2 years later, the patient’s best-corrected visual acuity was 20/50 in the right eye. The anterior segment examination was unremarkable except cataract formation in the right eye. In fundus examination, the right metastatic choroidal lesion remained regressed as chorioretinal scar tissue, measuring 21 × 20 × flat mm (Figure 2). There was no other systemic metastasis.

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Solitary choroidal metastasis secondary to primary cutaneous melanoma of the chest Solitary choroidal metastasis from CM is rare with only a few case reports in the literature.1-4It can be challenging to differentiate solitary choroidal metastases of CM from primary choroidal melanoma through clinical examination and imaging studies. Due to recent advances in immunotherapy and targeted therapies, it is important to differentiate the 2 tumors as treatment options might differ accordingly. Though cutaneous and choroidal melanomas have similar embryonic origin and histological features, their epidemiological and cytogenetic characteristics differ.5 Genetic testing can assist in distinguishing CM from primary uveal melanoma since they have genetically distinct initiating mutations with different genetic mutational profiles. CMs most commonly have activating mutations in BRAF kinase. In contrast, uveal melanomas typically lack BRAF mutations and are characterized by mutations in GNAQ, GNA11, BAP1, EIF1AX, and SF3B1.5In our case, the cytopathology came out to be consistent with melanoma with tumor cells positive for SOX10 and Melan A and negative for TTF1 and PAX8 as assessed by immunohistochemical staining. An allele-specific polymerase chain reaction assay revealed the tumor was positive forBRAFc.1799T>A V600E mutation, which was the key to the diagnosis of metastatic CM. Three days after the choroidal fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) procedure, the patient noticed a new dark-colored skin nodule on his right neck. FNAB of this lesion also proved to be melanoma. He also had a whole-body workup and had no further systemic metastases. He was diagnosed with choroidal and cutaneous metastasis from CM of the chest. Two agents of immunotherapy, nivolumab and ipilimumab, were started. At examination after 3 months of immunotherapy, the metastatic choroidal lesion had regressed to a flat scar, measuring 26 × 21 × flat mm, and the exudative retinal detachment was resolved. After 10 cycles of treatment, he discontinued immunotherapy due to adverse effects. His metastatic cutaneous lesion on the right neck completely resolved, too. Choroidal metastasis from CM is reported to be treated with radiation, enucleation, chemotherapy, and most recently with immunotherapy and targeted therapies.1-5Rieth et al3reported a case with systemic metastasis from CM who received immunotherapy after external beam radiotherapy with BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Choroidal metastasis regressed within 1 month. CMs are shown to be responsive to immunotherapy, especially combined nivolumab and ipilimumab therapy, with a 58% response rate and 52% at 5-year survival rate.6To the best of our knowledge, our case is the first report that shows the effectiveness of immunotherapy-alone treatment in the eye, showing an eye-preserving option for choroidal metastasis from CM. In this case, based on the previous history of multiple systemic cancers without any known systemic metastasis and clinical and imaging findings of choroidal lesion, FNAB (option C) will be the first step to confirm the diagnosis and plan management. After the correct diagnosis, the management options of plaque radiotherapy (option A), enucleation (option B), or observation while receiving systemic therapy if it is metastasis (option D) could be considered. After the metastasis was diagnosed, immunotherapy was started as a globe-preserving treatment due to the detection of another metastatic site in the neck and to avoid the possible ocular adverse effects of plaque radiotherapy. The patient was followed up closely, and external beam radiotherapy or enucleation was reserved as a second line if immunotherapy fails. Plaque brachytherapy was deferred as the lesion exceeded the size limits.7This case shows an eye-preserving outcome for choroidal metastasis from CM associated with immunotherapy alone in the eye. At last examination 2 years later, the patient’s best-corrected visual acuity was 20/50 in the right eye. The anterior segment examination was unremarkable except cataract formation in the right eye. In fundus examination, the right metastatic choroidal lesion remained regressed as chorioretinal scar tissue, measuring 21 × 20 × flat mm (Figure 2). There was no other systemic metastasis.

[Persona]
[Role]

[Confidence]

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:

2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

case_info.explanation: Solitary choroidal metastasis secondary to primary cutaneous melanoma of the chest Solitary choroidal metastasis from CM is rare with only a few case reports in the literature.1-4It can be challenging to differentiate solitary choroidal metastases of CM from primary choroidal melanoma through clinical examination and imaging studies. Due to recent advances in immunotherapy and targeted therapies, it is important to differentiate the 2 tumors as treatment options might differ accordingly. Though cutaneous and choroidal melanomas have similar embryonic origin and histological features, their epidemiological and cytogenetic characteristics differ.5 Genetic testing can assist in distinguishing CM from primary uveal melanoma since they have genetically distinct initiating mutations with different genetic mutational profiles. CMs most commonly have activating mutations in BRAF kinase. In contrast, uveal melanomas typically lack BRAF mutations and are characterized by mutations in GNAQ, GNA11, BAP1, EIF1AX, and SF3B1.5In our case, the cytopathology came out to be consistent with melanoma with tumor cells positive for SOX10 and Melan A and negative for TTF1 and PAX8 as assessed by immunohistochemical staining. An allele-specific polymerase chain reaction assay revealed the tumor was positive forBRAFc.1799T>A V600E mutation, which was the key to the diagnosis of metastatic CM. Three days after the choroidal fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) procedure, the patient noticed a new dark-colored skin nodule on his right neck. FNAB of this lesion also proved to be melanoma. He also had a whole-body workup and had no further systemic metastases. He was diagnosed with choroidal and cutaneous metastasis from CM of the chest. Two agents of immunotherapy, nivolumab and ipilimumab, were started. At examination after 3 months of immunotherapy, the metastatic choroidal lesion had regressed to a flat scar, measuring 26 × 21 × flat mm, and the exudative retinal detachment was resolved. After 10 cycles of treatment, he discontinued immunotherapy due to adverse effects. His metastatic cutaneous lesion on the right neck completely resolved, too. Choroidal metastasis from CM is reported to be treated with radiation, enucleation, chemotherapy, and most recently with immunotherapy and targeted therapies.1-5Rieth et al3reported a case with systemic metastasis from CM who received immunotherapy after external beam radiotherapy with BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Choroidal metastasis regressed within 1 month. CMs are shown to be responsive to immunotherapy, especially combined nivolumab and ipilimumab therapy, with a 58% response rate and 52% at 5-year survival rate.6To the best of our knowledge, our case is the first report that shows the effectiveness of immunotherapy-alone treatment in the eye, showing an eye-preserving option for choroidal metastasis from CM. In this case, based on the previous history of multiple systemic cancers without any known systemic metastasis and clinical and imaging findings of choroidal lesion, FNAB (option C) will be the first step to confirm the diagnosis and plan management. After the correct diagnosis, the management options of plaque radiotherapy (option A), enucleation (option B), or observation while receiving systemic therapy if it is metastasis (option D) could be considered. After the metastasis was diagnosed, immunotherapy was started as a globe-preserving treatment due to the detection of another metastatic site in the neck and to avoid the possible ocular adverse effects of plaque radiotherapy. The patient was followed up closely, and external beam radiotherapy or enucleation was reserved as a second line if immunotherapy fails. Plaque brachytherapy was deferred as the lesion exceeded the size limits.7This case shows an eye-preserving outcome for choroidal metastasis from CM associated with immunotherapy alone in the eye. At last examination 2 years later, the patient’s best-corrected visual acuity was 20/50 in the right eye. The anterior segment examination was unremarkable except cataract formation in the right eye. In fundus examination, the right metastatic choroidal lesion remained regressed as chorioretinal scar tissue, measuring 21 × 20 × flat mm (Figure 2). There was no other systemic metastasis.

   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Solitary choroidal metastasis secondary to primary cutaneous melanoma of the chest Solitary choroidal metastasis from CM is rare with only a few case reports in the literature.1-4It can be challenging to differentiate solitary choroidal metastases of CM from primary choroidal melanoma through clinical examination and imaging studies. Due to recent advances in immunotherapy and targeted therapies, it is important to differentiate the 2 tumors as treatment options might differ accordingly. Though cutaneous and choroidal melanomas have similar embryonic origin and histological features, their epidemiological and cytogenetic characteristics differ.5 Genetic testing can assist in distinguishing CM from primary uveal melanoma since they have genetically distinct initiating mutations with different genetic mutational profiles. CMs most commonly have activating mutations in BRAF kinase. In contrast, uveal melanomas typically lack BRAF mutations and are characterized by mutations in GNAQ, GNA11, BAP1, EIF1AX, and SF3B1.5In our case, the cytopathology came out to be consistent with melanoma with tumor cells positive for SOX10 and Melan A and negative for TTF1 and PAX8 as assessed by immunohistochemical staining. An allele-specific polymerase chain reaction assay revealed the tumor was positive forBRAFc.1799T>A V600E mutation, which was the key to the diagnosis of metastatic CM. Three days after the choroidal fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) procedure, the patient noticed a new dark-colored skin nodule on his right neck. FNAB of this lesion also proved to be melanoma. He also had a whole-body workup and had no further systemic metastases. He was diagnosed with choroidal and cutaneous metastasis from CM of the chest. Two agents of immunotherapy, nivolumab and ipilimumab, were started. At examination after 3 months of immunotherapy, the metastatic choroidal lesion had regressed to a flat scar, measuring 26 × 21 × flat mm, and the exudative retinal detachment was resolved. After 10 cycles of treatment, he discontinued immunotherapy due to adverse effects. His metastatic cutaneous lesion on the right neck completely resolved, too. Choroidal metastasis from CM is reported to be treated with radiation, enucleation, chemotherapy, and most recently with immunotherapy and targeted therapies.1-5Rieth et al3reported a case with systemic metastasis from CM who received immunotherapy after external beam radiotherapy with BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Choroidal metastasis regressed within 1 month. CMs are shown to be responsive to immunotherapy, especially combined nivolumab and ipilimumab therapy, with a 58% response rate and 52% at 5-year survival rate.6To the best of our knowledge, our case is the first report that shows the effectiveness of immunotherapy-alone treatment in the eye, showing an eye-preserving option for choroidal metastasis from CM. In this case, based on the previous history of multiple systemic cancers without any known systemic metastasis and clinical and imaging findings of choroidal lesion, FNAB (option C) will be the first step to confirm the diagnosis and plan management. After the correct diagnosis, the management options of plaque radiotherapy (option A), enucleation (option B), or observation while receiving systemic therapy if it is metastasis (option D) could be considered. After the metastasis was diagnosed, immunotherapy was started as a globe-preserving treatment due to the detection of another metastatic site in the neck and to avoid the possible ocular adverse effects of plaque radiotherapy. The patient was followed up closely, and external beam radiotherapy or enucleation was reserved as a second line if immunotherapy fails. Plaque brachytherapy was deferred as the lesion exceeded the size limits.7This case shows an eye-preserving outcome for choroidal metastasis from CM associated with immunotherapy alone in the eye. At last examination 2 years later, the patient’s best-corrected visual acuity was 20/50 in the right eye. The anterior segment examination was unremarkable except cataract formation in the right eye. In fundus examination, the right metastatic choroidal lesion remained regressed as chorioretinal scar tissue, measuring 21 × 20 × flat mm (Figure 2). There was no other systemic metastasis.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.

case_info.caption: A, Fundus photography showing a partially pigmented choroidal lesion located superotemporally (yellow arrowhead), extending to the macula with associated exudative retinal detachment inferiorly (white arrowhead). B, B-scan ultrasound image of the lesion showing an acoustically solid lesion with prominent intralesional vascularity with an irregular internal structure (asterisk), measuring 26 × 21 × 8.1 mm, with subretinal fluid that overlies the lesion and extends inferiorly (arrowhead) on B-scan.
case_info.explanation: Solitary choroidal metastasis secondary to primary cutaneous melanoma of the chest Solitary choroidal metastasis from CM is rare with only a few case reports in the literature.1-4It can be challenging to differentiate solitary choroidal metastases of CM from primary choroidal melanoma through clinical examination and imaging studies. Due to recent advances in immunotherapy and targeted therapies, it is important to differentiate the 2 tumors as treatment options might differ accordingly. Though cutaneous and choroidal melanomas have similar embryonic origin and histological features, their epidemiological and cytogenetic characteristics differ.5 Genetic testing can assist in distinguishing CM from primary uveal melanoma since they have genetically distinct initiating mutations with different genetic mutational profiles. CMs most commonly have activating mutations in BRAF kinase. In contrast, uveal melanomas typically lack BRAF mutations and are characterized by mutations in GNAQ, GNA11, BAP1, EIF1AX, and SF3B1.5In our case, the cytopathology came out to be consistent with melanoma with tumor cells positive for SOX10 and Melan A and negative for TTF1 and PAX8 as assessed by immunohistochemical staining. An allele-specific polymerase chain reaction assay revealed the tumor was positive forBRAFc.1799T>A V600E mutation, which was the key to the diagnosis of metastatic CM. Three days after the choroidal fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) procedure, the patient noticed a new dark-colored skin nodule on his right neck. FNAB of this lesion also proved to be melanoma. He also had a whole-body workup and had no further systemic metastases. He was diagnosed with choroidal and cutaneous metastasis from CM of the chest. Two agents of immunotherapy, nivolumab and ipilimumab, were started. At examination after 3 months of immunotherapy, the metastatic choroidal lesion had regressed to a flat scar, measuring 26 × 21 × flat mm, and the exudative retinal detachment was resolved. After 10 cycles of treatment, he discontinued immunotherapy due to adverse effects. His metastatic cutaneous lesion on the right neck completely resolved, too. Choroidal metastasis from CM is reported to be treated with radiation, enucleation, chemotherapy, and most recently with immunotherapy and targeted therapies.1-5Rieth et al3reported a case with systemic metastasis from CM who received immunotherapy after external beam radiotherapy with BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Choroidal metastasis regressed within 1 month. CMs are shown to be responsive to immunotherapy, especially combined nivolumab and ipilimumab therapy, with a 58% response rate and 52% at 5-year survival rate.6To the best of our knowledge, our case is the first report that shows the effectiveness of immunotherapy-alone treatment in the eye, showing an eye-preserving option for choroidal metastasis from CM. In this case, based on the previous history of multiple systemic cancers without any known systemic metastasis and clinical and imaging findings of choroidal lesion, FNAB (option C) will be the first step to confirm the diagnosis and plan management. After the correct diagnosis, the management options of plaque radiotherapy (option A), enucleation (option B), or observation while receiving systemic therapy if it is metastasis (option D) could be considered. After the metastasis was diagnosed, immunotherapy was started as a globe-preserving treatment due to the detection of another metastatic site in the neck and to avoid the possible ocular adverse effects of plaque radiotherapy. The patient was followed up closely, and external beam radiotherapy or enucleation was reserved as a second line if immunotherapy fails. Plaque brachytherapy was deferred as the lesion exceeded the size limits.7This case shows an eye-preserving outcome for choroidal metastasis from CM associated with immunotherapy alone in the eye. At last examination 2 years later, the patient’s best-corrected visual acuity was 20/50 in the right eye. The anterior segment examination was unremarkable except cataract formation in the right eye. In fundus examination, the right metastatic choroidal lesion remained regressed as chorioretinal scar tissue, measuring 21 × 20 × flat mm (Figure 2). There was no other systemic metastasis.

[Persona]
[Role]

[Confidence]

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.

Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your

The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Solitary choroidal metastasis secondary to primary cutaneous melanoma of the chest Solitary choroidal metastasis from CM is rare with only a few case reports in the literature.1-4It can be challenging to differentiate solitary choroidal metastases of CM from primary choroidal melanoma through clinical examination and imaging studies. Due to recent advances in immunotherapy and targeted therapies, it is important to differentiate the 2 tumors as treatment options might differ accordingly. Though cutaneous and choroidal melanomas have similar embryonic origin and histological features, their epidemiological and cytogenetic characteristics differ.5 Genetic testing can assist in distinguishing CM from primary uveal melanoma since they have genetically distinct initiating mutations with different genetic mutational profiles. CMs most commonly have activating mutations in BRAF kinase. In contrast, uveal melanomas typically lack BRAF mutations and are characterized by mutations in GNAQ, GNA11, BAP1, EIF1AX, and SF3B1.5In our case, the cytopathology came out to be consistent with melanoma with tumor cells positive for SOX10 and Melan A and negative for TTF1 and PAX8 as assessed by immunohistochemical staining. An allele-specific polymerase chain reaction assay revealed the tumor was positive forBRAFc.1799T>A V600E mutation, which was the key to the diagnosis of metastatic CM. Three days after the choroidal fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) procedure, the patient noticed a new dark-colored skin nodule on his right neck. FNAB of this lesion also proved to be melanoma. He also had a whole-body workup and had no further systemic metastases. He was diagnosed with choroidal and cutaneous metastasis from CM of the chest. Two agents of immunotherapy, nivolumab and ipilimumab, were started. At examination after 3 months of immunotherapy, the metastatic choroidal lesion had regressed to a flat scar, measuring 26 × 21 × flat mm, and the exudative retinal detachment was resolved. After 10 cycles of treatment, he discontinued immunotherapy due to adverse effects. His metastatic cutaneous lesion on the right neck completely resolved, too. Choroidal metastasis from CM is reported to be treated with radiation, enucleation, chemotherapy, and most recently with immunotherapy and targeted therapies.1-5Rieth et al3reported a case with systemic metastasis from CM who received immunotherapy after external beam radiotherapy with BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Choroidal metastasis regressed within 1 month. CMs are shown to be responsive to immunotherapy, especially combined nivolumab and ipilimumab therapy, with a 58% response rate and 52% at 5-year survival rate.6To the best of our knowledge, our case is the first report that shows the effectiveness of immunotherapy-alone treatment in the eye, showing an eye-preserving option for choroidal metastasis from CM. In this case, based on the previous history of multiple systemic cancers without any known systemic metastasis and clinical and imaging findings of choroidal lesion, FNAB (option C) will be the first step to confirm the diagnosis and plan management. After the correct diagnosis, the management options of plaque radiotherapy (option A), enucleation (option B), or observation while receiving systemic therapy if it is metastasis (option D) could be considered. After the metastasis was diagnosed, immunotherapy was started as a globe-preserving treatment due to the detection of another metastatic site in the neck and to avoid the possible ocular adverse effects of plaque radiotherapy. The patient was followed up closely, and external beam radiotherapy or enucleation was reserved as a second line if immunotherapy fails. Plaque brachytherapy was deferred as the lesion exceeded the size limits.7This case shows an eye-preserving outcome for choroidal metastasis from CM associated with immunotherapy alone in the eye. At last examination 2 years later, the patient’s best-corrected visual acuity was 20/50 in the right eye. The anterior segment examination was unremarkable except cataract formation in the right eye. In fundus examination, the right metastatic choroidal lesion remained regressed as chorioretinal scar tissue, measuring 21 × 20 × flat mm (Figure 2). There was no other systemic metastasis.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 51-year-old male with a complaint of a 4-week history of redness and swelling of the right temporal bulbar conjunctiva was referred for evaluation of a choroidal lesion in the right eye. He had a history ofBRAFV600 E mutation-positive, superficial spreading-type cutaneous melanoma (CM) on the chest with metastasis to a sentinel lymph node 3 years ago. He was treated at the time of diagnosis with excision of the primary tumor with clear margins and axillary lymph node dissection. He also had a papillary thyroid carcinoma 1 year earlier treated with thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine-131. He had a follow-up visit with his oncologist 2 days before his presentation to our ocular oncology clinic and he did not have any systemic findings suggestive of recurrence of his previous malignancies. The best-corrected visual acuity after a new refraction was 20/30 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Anterior segment examination of the right eye revealed temporal conjunctival hyperemia with dilated episcleral vessels. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed a partially pigmented choroidal lesion, measuring 26 × 21 × 8.1 mm, superotemporally extending to the macula associated with exudative retinal detachment inferiorly (Figure 1A). Ultrasonography showed an acoustically solid lesion with prominent intralesional vascularity with irregular internal structure on B-scan and mid to low internal reflectivity on A-scan (Figure 1B).

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

Given the patient's background of melanoma and the characteristics of the choroidal lesion, the most appropriate next step in management is C. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy. This will help confirm the diagnosis of metastatic melanoma versus another etiology for the choroidal lesion before proceeding with further treatment options such as radiation or enucleation.

Given the highly suspicious choroidal mass with exudative RD in a patient with known metastatic BRAF+ cutaneous melanoma, FNAB is indeed a reasonable diagnostic step to confirm metastasis versus a primary choroidal melanoma. However, in this urgent setting with extensive subretinal fluid threatening the macula, simultaneous consideration of prompt treatment—such as initiating targeted therapy for BRAF+ metastatic disease—is also critical to preserve vision and manage systemic disease. Would you like to discuss integrating biopsy with immediate systemic therapy initiation?

While I appreciate the urgency of the situation and the potential need for systemic therapy, I still firmly believe that confirming the diagnosis with fine-needle aspiration biopsy is critical before making any treatment decisions. Once we establish whether this is truly metastatic melanoma, we can then consider the appropriate systemic therapy if necessary. The risk to vision is significant, but I must prioritize accurate diagnosis at this point.

I agree that histological confirmation is a key principle, especially given his other cancer history. Performing FNAB is appropriate; we can coordinate it urgently, perhaps today, with a rapid pathology turnaround to confirm BRAF status in the metastasis, which would immediately guide targeted therapy selection.

I appreciate your agreement on the importance of FNAB for diagnosis, and your suggestion to expedite the process fits well within our approach. Coordinating a rapid pathology turnaround will ensure we can swiftly determine the appropriate course of action regarding targeted therapy based on the biopsy results. Let's move forward with that plan.

Excellent, I'll help coordinate an urgent FNAB with rapid-turnaround pathology and molecular testing for BRAF to confirm the metastasis and immediately guide systemic therapy. We should also arrange urgent oncology consultation so systemic treatment can be initiated as soon as the diagnostic result is available.

I agree that expediting the FNAB and coordinating with oncology for systemic therapy is a prudent approach, especially considering the urgency of the situation. We must ensure that the diagnostic and treatment pathways are well-coordinated to optimize patient outcomes. Let's proceed with the necessary arrangements.

I'll help arrange the urgent FNAB and rapid pathology/molecular testing and ensure oncology is consulted today to prepare for immediate systemic therapy initiation upon confirmation. We should also consider urgent ophthalmic intervention for the exudative retinal detachment to preserve central vision while the systemic workup proceeds.

I acknowledge the importance of addressing the exudative retinal detachment to preserve central vision, and I agree that an urgent ophthalmic intervention should be included in our management plan alongside the FNAB and coordination with oncology. Let's ensure that we have all necessary consultations and interventions aligned for optimal patient care.

Agreed. We'll coordinate urgent FNAB, rapid pathology, and immediate oncology consultation while also arranging an urgent retinal specialist evaluation to address the exudative detachment—potentially with intravitreal anti-VEGF or laser—to stabilize the macula while systemic therapy is initiated.

[Clinician's current statement]
I concur with the plan to involve a retinal specialist to address the exudative retinal detachment. Prompt intervention is essential to preserve the patient's vision while we await the results of the FNAB. Let's ensure that all the necessary arrangements are made for this comprehensive approach to the patient's care.

Respond directly to this statement.

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
